## Eight practitioner assumptions, negated

1. **Conv gains add up across parallel edges into a node.** If false, a conv on a sibling edge saturates the node, so a second conv or skip on the other fan-in edge adds less (hypotheses 1, 3, 10, 11, 18, 27).
2. **Skip is always a safe, helpful addition.** If false, skip is worth much more when the node has no strong alternative route, and little when a conv already carries the signal (2, 12, 28).
3. **The direct edge 3 is independent of the deeper routes.** If false, the direct edge substitutes for them: deeper conv edits gain more when edge 3 is `none` and less when it is skip (4, 26).
4. **Upstream convs make downstream convs more useful.** If false, a downstream conv is worth only as much as the signal reaching it, so its gain collapses when the upstream edge is `none` and recovers after a pool (5, 7, 8, 9, 19, 20, 22, 23, 24).
5. **Stacked avg-pools always oversmooth, and a pool is just a weak op.** If false, a conv after a pool is worth more because it restores features, while pool-on-pool is the case that really hurts (6, 21, 25, 29).
6. **3x3 beats 1x1 whatever it replaces.** If false, the upgrade value depends on what is replaced, so replacing `none` gains much more than replacing skip or a conv (13, 14, 15, 30).
7. **`none` is uniformly the worst op, so removing it always pays the same.** If false, the payoff depends on whether the edge is the node's only input (12, 15, 30).
8. **Pool to skip is a marginal swap.** If false, replacing a pool with skip on serial edges gives a consistent gain, because it removes smoothing from the chain (16, 17).

All 30 hypotheses below come from these negations. The signs are my beliefs and have not been tested against benchmark data.
